LOSS OF LIFE FOLLOWING MAN OVERBOARD FROM P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST
8. A red warning sign on the port side walkway approaching the stern stated, “Authorized personnel

lines.text: only beyond this point." The starboard side walkway approaching the stern had no such visual
warning sign. Furthermore, there was no list of personnel authorized to access the stern on the
vessel (or from the company).
9. Chains with red signs that said "Employees Only" protect passengers from approaching the stern
on both sides of the main deck. On 07AUG12 and 09OCT12, visiting Coast Guard investigators
found these protective chains hanging from the bulkhead of the vessel instead of in place across
the walkways. Captain
stated that policy required the chains to remain attached across
the walkways, but that the crew often neglected to put them back in place when they went
through. No written policy could be found to support Captain
assertion.
10. An area of 54 inches between the paddlewheel diagonal support posts and the aftermost bulkhead
of the vessel was not protected by a railing or by a chain. This was the location where Mr.
Staples fell in. An additional length of 10 feet on the port side stern was not protected by railings
or other suitable guards to prevent someone from falling overboard. For additional detail, see
Vessel Stern Schematic and Paddlewheel Support Arm Photo on pages 8 and 9, respectively.
11. From December 2010 until May 2011, P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST underwent a complete
propulsion system modification in which the entire stern was cut away and new bearing supports,
deck plates, and a cosmetic paddle wheel were installed. MSU Portland Inspector
was the lead Coast Guard inspector for the project. Mr.
was the
vessel's representative during the project.
12. Plans were submitted by the Naval Architect Mr.
of Chesapeake Shipbuilding and
approved by Marine Safety Center. The plans did not indicate a railing arrangement, nor were
there plans for a railing configuration onboard the vessel. The Marine Safety Center will review
lat MSC, "the designer
handrails only if the information is provided. According to
provides [us] the overall construction of the vessel rather than details which are often left up to an
outfitting decision: the owner may like the look of one handrail vs. another and that decision
hasn't been made when construction begins."
13. On 04MAR11, MSU Inspector
found the paddlewheel installed and indicated
that all was satisfactory. During the project, Mr.
discussed the
and Mr.
railing configuration and decided jointly that certain railings would not be included on the stern.
As river debris frequently lodges in the paddlewheel planks, the risk of this debris getting caught
in the associated railings outweighed the risk of someone falling overboard from the stern. The
decision was made to make access to the stern authorized only to engineers working on the
hydraulic machinery.
14. There was an eye-hook on the aftermost railing stanchion. This stanchion was the last stanchion
of existing railing before the 10 foot unprotected area on the port side stern began. According to
Mr.
the eye-hook was a connection point for a chain that was supposed to be
designed to keep people away from the stern. The chain was not in place, nor had it ever been in
place. Mr.
assumed responsibility for not having the chain in place. Even if the chain
had been in place on the night of the incident, it would not have prevented Mr. Staples from
falling overboard, as he did not fall directly off the stern.
15. An outdoor flood light was attached to the bulkhead above the machinery for the port engine on
the paddlewheel support arm, but witnesses conflicted as to whether the light was on at the time
of the incident. No other evidence exists to determine whether or not it was in operation. The
light was wired on a separate switch from the rest of the deck lights so that it does not come into
operation when the main deck lights are activated.
